stories.title: From the Mayflower to Texas
stories.dek: Edward Doty crossed on the Mayflower in 1620. His descendants spent two centuries in New Jersey before one of them headed west.
places: Piscataway, Middlesex County, New Jersey, USA
Scotch Plains, Union County, New Jersey, USA
Long Branch, Monmouth County, New Jersey, USA
stories.html:
Edward Doty was one of the 102 passengers on the Mayflower in 1620. He came as a servant of Stephen Hopkins and signed the Mayflower Compact. The next year he and another servant, Edward Leister, fought what is remembered as the colony's first duel. Both men were wounded, and the colony punished them for it.

Doty became a free man and a landowner in Plymouth. In 1635 he married Faith Clarke, who had come from Ipswich, Suffolk as a girl. He died in Plymouth on 23 August 1655, and Faith lived on until 1675.

Their son Samuel Doty, born in Plymouth about 1643, moved to Piscataway in East Jersey. He married there in 1678, and the family stayed in New Jersey for the next five generations, spelling the name Doty or Doughty:

  • Samuel Doty, born in Piscataway in 1679
  • Moses Doughty, born 1702, who died at Scotch Plains in 1775, on the eve of the Revolution
  • Mercy Doty, who married Reuben Compton about 1759
  • William Compton and his daughter Mary Ann Compton, who married Samuel A. Drake in 1828

Their son Joseph Cullen Drake was born at Long Branch on the Jersey Shore in 1834. He broke the pattern. He married in Illinois and died in Hamilton County, Texas, in 1904. His daughter Susie married Mark R. Winters.

What's proven:

  • The first five generations are well supported. Edward → Samuel → Samuel → Moses → Mercy is covered by the Doty-Doten Family in America (1897) and by Moses Doty's own will. In 1775 that will left £50 to "Daughter, Marcy, the wife of Ruben Compton".
  • William Compton → Mary Ann Compton → the Drakes is a little less certain. William's mother-in-law's will names "Daughter, Susannah Compton", and Joseph Cullen Drake appears in Samuel Drake's household in the 1850 census.
  • Two links are still inferences: William as Reuben's son, and Mary Ann as William's daughter. Estate papers in Somerset County, New Jersey, are the place to prove them.

Before applying to the Mayflower Society, check the line against its published Doty volume (Mayflower Families, vol. 11).

stories.title: How Feigenwinter became Winters
stories.dek: An 1890 county history names Henry and Sarah Winters as the parents of George Thomas Winters. The Swiss name before that is still a lead.
places: Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina, USA
stories.html:
In 1890 a county history of Cross County, Arkansas, included a biography of a farmer named H. C. Winters. It said he was "the eldest son of Henry and Sarah (Rinfrow) Winters", from North Carolina and Tennessee respectively.

Henry had been a soldier in the War of 1812. In 1828 he married Sarah Renfro, his second wife, and moved to Morgan County, Alabama. About five years later they moved on to Tippah County, Mississippi. Henry died there in 1852.

Sarah raised six children: H. C., J. J., Thomas, William C., Mary E. and Sarah J. She was a Methodist. She went west to Texas with her son George Thomas Winters, born in Alabama in 1832, and died there in 1880.

George Thomas was in Tippah County for the 1850 and 1870 censuses. By 1880 he had taken his family to Coryell County, Texas. He died at Evant in 1908.

The Swiss question: War of 1812 papers attached on Ancestry spell Henry's name "Figinwinters" and "Henry F. Winters". That suggests the family was once Feigenwinter, from Reinach near Basel. The Feigenwinters are recorded in Reinach from 1463. Some family trees make Henry the son of Christoph "Stoffel" Feigenwinter, who settled in Salisbury, North Carolina, and Barbara Faw.

What's proven: Henry and Sarah as George Thomas's parents now rest on the 1890 biography, written while their children were alive. The Feigenwinter link and the Swiss generations are not proven yet. Henry's War of 1812 file at the National Archives would be the next record to get.

stories.title: The postmaster of Stringtown
stories.dek: The Winters family reached Indian Territory just as it became Oklahoma, and stayed in Atoka County for half a century.
places: Justice Precinct 4, Lampasas County, Texas, USA
Poteau, Le Flore County, Oklahoma, USA
stories.html:
Mark R. Winters was born in Mississippi in 1869. As a boy he moved with his family to central Texas. He was in Coryell County in 1880 and in Lampasas County in 1900 with his wife Susie and their children.

Before 1910 they moved north to Stringtown, in Atoka County, Oklahoma. Oklahoma had become a state in November 1907. On 28 November 1908, Mark was appointed postmaster of Stringtown, which the U.S. postmaster appointment records confirm. The family stayed in Stringtown through the 1940 census.

Their son Marion P. Winters was born in Texas in 1896. He registered for the World War I draft in Atoka County. The Army Transport Service passenger lists show him shipping out of New York on 20 June 1918, headed overseas with the Army. He came home and married Ina Perry, and they were back in Stringtown by 1935.

Marion and Ina's son Richard Lee Winters was born in November 1926. He grew up in Stringtown and registered for the draft there in 1946. On 7 July 1951 he married Joyce Yvonne Creamer in Durant, where she had been born. They later lived in Poteau, in Le Flore County.

What's proven: Every step here is backed by census, draft, postmaster or passenger records.

stories.title: The Tippecanoe tradition
stories.dek: Family trees say Jack Callahan died at Tippecanoe in 1811. The records tell a more tangled story.
stories.html:
Before dawn on 7 November 1811, warriors of the confederacy led by the Shawnee brothers Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa attacked Governor William Henry Harrison's army. Harrison's men were camped on the Tippecanoe River in Indiana Territory. Dozens of his men died, and the battle helped bring on the War of 1812.

Family trees say John "Jack" Callahan was among the dead. His daughter Lavica Jane had married George R. Haley in Kentucky in 1809. The Haleys later settled in Warren County, Tennessee, and their daughter Rhoda married into the Smithson family.

What the records say: No Callahan appears on the surviving Tippecanoe muster rolls or casualty lists. The family trees give Jack's mother as Sukey Brock. But a 1773 Virginia court record names an Edward Callihan living with a Susanna Brock, and Clay County, Kentucky, compilations list Edward and Sukey's children as William, Jennie, Elizabeth, Zelphia, Charlotte and Isaac. There's no John.

So Lavica may well be a Callahan from this Clay County family, perhaps a granddaughter of Edward and Sukey, but the line as the trees draw it doesn't hold up.

What's proven: Not yet. George Haley's marriage bond from about 1809, filed in Lincoln, Pulaski or Madison County, Kentucky, might name Lavica's father.

stories.title: The Chief Red Bird tradition
stories.dek: A family story connects the Brocks to a Cherokee leader. Records from 1797 tell a different story.
stories.html:
Many family trees, ours included, said that Aaron Brock was the Cherokee leader known as Chief Red Bird, or Totsu'hwa, and that he died on the Red Bird River in Clay County, Kentucky, in 1820. His daughter Sukey Brock is a well-documented Clay County pioneer.

Stories like this are common in Appalachian families, and they're part of family memory. Here is what the records say:

  • Red Bird died earlier. On 17 March 1797, Tennessee Governor John Sevier wrote to the governor of Kentucky about the murder of the Cherokee Red Bird and a companion. A Kentucky historical marker at Oneida tells the same story of a killing over furs.
  • Brock family researchers found no link. They have found no evidence that Aaron Brock and Red Bird were the same man. There was also more than one Cherokee named Red Bird.
  • DNA points to Europe. The Brock DNA project traces the family's direct male line to a European ancestor, George Brock of Albemarle County, Virginia.

A relative, Ruthie Rawlings, filed a "Native American application", probably to the Eastern Cherokee (Guion Miller) rolls of 1906–1909. About two-thirds of those claims were rejected. Finding hers on the National Archives microfilm (M1104) would show how this story was told a century ago, and how the government ruled on it.

What's proven: The Red Bird identification is contradicted by the records. Aaron Brock's own parentage of Sukey is also unproven.

stories.title: A lieutenant on the Georgia frontier
stories.dek: Robert Stewart's own pension application tells his story, from New Bern to the Siege of Augusta.
places: New Bern, Craven County, North Carolina, USA
Six Mile, Pickens County, South Carolina, USA
stories.html:
On 11 March 1833, an 84-year-old man named Robert Stewart went before a court in Pickens District, South Carolina, to apply for a Revolutionary War pension. His sworn statement survives.

He said he was born near New Bern, North Carolina. His father moved the family to Cumberland County, NC, and then to the Georgia backcountry, which became Wilkes County in 1777. Robert married Nancy Holloway in Columbia County, Georgia, a few years before the war. A brother-in-law, William Holloway, later swore he had been at the wedding.

When the war came, Robert served in the Georgia militia. He was first a lieutenant under Captain Burke at a fort on the Broad River, then a private under Dooly, Clarke and others, including at the Siege of Augusta. In 1784 Colonel Elijah Clarke signed a Georgia bounty certificate for his service. The pension was rejected, as many backcountry militia claims were. Robert died on 8 December 1835.

The family trees name his father as Capt. John Stewart, killed by a raiding party in Wilkes County in December 1777, whose sons filed a claim against Georgia in 1786. That would fit a frontier family, but it hasn't been confirmed.

What's proven: Robert's birth, marriage, service and death come from his own pension file (R10167). His father's name and death, and the link down to the Creamers through William Stewart, still need records. Older trees made the family descend from a "Sir John Stewart, 4th Baronet" and Lady Jane Douglas. We've removed that line because it is impossible: Lady Jane married in 1746, at 48, and her only children were twins born in 1748.

stories.title: Sicily to Kansas City and Denver
stories.dek: The Palmisano family came from Termini Imerese, a fishing and market town on Sicily's north coast.
places: Kansas City, Jackson County, Missouri, USA
stories.html:
Termini Imerese sits on the Tyrrhenian coast about 35 km east of Palermo. It has a hilltop old town above a harbor. The tree places several families there through the 1700s and 1800s, all of them neighbors and in-laws:

  • the Palmisanos: Fillipo, born 1762, and his son Vincenzo, 1799–1857
  • the Cefalù/Ciofalo family: Gaspare Ciofalo, who died in Termini in 1776
  • the Carusos: Nicolo Caruso and his daughter Rosaria "Rosa", who married Vincenzo Palmisano

Filippo Palmesana was born in January 1846 and emigrated in 1881. His wife Antonia followed in 1885. Their daughter Reosa was born in Kansas City in January 1888. By 1900 the family was in Denver, where Reosa married Joseph Marzyck. She lived in Denver until 1983.

If you are in Sicily: Termini Imerese is the town to visit. Cefalù, one of the island's most visited towns, is 35 km further east along the coast. The tree's Cefalù and Ciofalo ancestors carry its name. The Chiesa Madre (mother church) of Termini Imerese holds the parish registers where these baptisms and marriages would have been recorded.

What's proven: Filippo and Antonia's arrival and Reosa's American life are documented by censuses. Their surnames point to Termini Imerese: Palmisano and Cira are both common among emigrants from the town. But no record has named their hometown yet, so the Termini generations above Filippo are a hypothesis.

How to check: Termini Imerese's 1846 birth register is free to view on Antenati. January births are near the front, and there's usually an alphabetical index at the back. If Filippo is there, his record names his father and his mother's maiden name. An older line from Carini, back to the 1500s, was removed because it rested on nothing but the common surname Caruso.

stories.title: Two families from Vienna
stories.dek: The Marzycks and the Papesches both came from Vienna, sixty years apart. They met in America.
stories.html:
John Marzyck was born in Vienna about 1810. He went into the "mercantile business" and ended up in Charleston, South Carolina, where he died of consumption (tuberculosis) in November 1868. His son Charles Francis Marzyck was born in Austria in 1851. Charles was naturalized in Colorado and lived in Denver with his Prussian-born wife, Mary Kasner. He died in San Francisco in 1910.

Their son Joseph, born in Colorado in 1887, made the Denver Post on 17 November 1906, at age 19, for losing his money. The clipping is attached to his record on Ancestry. Joseph married Reosa Palmesana, the daughter of Sicilian immigrants, and their daughter Mary Agnes was born in Denver in 1907.

Viktor Papesch was born in Vienna on 26 January 1905. He arrived in New York on 26 July 1930 and became a U.S. citizen in 1936. By 1940 he was living in Chicago with Mary Agnes and their son Roger. In 1955 Viktor made a trip back to Europe through Cherbourg and Le Havre. He lived to 101 and died in Wilmette, Illinois, in 2006. Mary Agnes died there two years later.

What's proven: Censuses, passenger lists, naturalization papers and Social Security records back up this story. Viktor's parents are listed as Ottokar Papesch and a woman whose surname was Hrdlička. Vienna's parish records would tell us more about them.

stories.title: The Polish families of Chicago
stories.dek: Three families sailed to Chicago between 1890 and 1910 and settled within a few miles of each other.
stories.html:
Teofil Pajrowski and his wife Joanna arrived from Poland in 1890 or 1891. Their daughter Sophie was born in Illinois in May 1891, soon after they arrived. They lived in Chicago's 16th Ward, on the Northwest Side.

William Kulik came over as a teenager between 1904 and 1907. His mother Albina arrived in 1904. William married Sophie, and their daughter Ester was born in Chicago in 1916.

Jan (John) Rusin sailed from Antwerp and landed in New York on 14 May 1907, at age 16. Katarzyna "Katie" Rapta made the same crossing in March 1910. Their records list them as Polish but also mention Austria. At the time there was no Polish state, and southern Poland (Galicia) was part of the Austrian Empire. They married in Chicago, and their son Frank was born on Christmas Day 1915.

Frank married Ester Kulik. In 1940 they were living in Leyden Township, west of the city, with their daughter Elaine. Elaine married Roger Papesch in 1960.

What's proven: Censuses, passenger lists, draft cards and naturalization indexes back up this story. The towns the families came from are the next thing to find: "Zlotnov" for Teofil and "Taine" for Albina, as the records spell them. Naturalization papers usually name the hometown.

stories.title: From Dorset to Texas
stories.dek: Martha Bell Palmer was born in a Dorset village where her mother's family had lived for three hundred years. She died in Texas.
stories.html:
The Lodders of Stour Provost, in north Dorset, are the deepest-rooted family in the tree. Three generations in a row named a son Gilbert:

  • Gilbert, born 1629
  • Gilbert, born 1666
  • Gilbert, born 1704

Their descendants George and Thomas Lodder stayed on the same land. Thomas's daughter Elizabeth, born in 1807, married John Palmer of nearby Child Okeford in 1829.

Their daughter Martha Bell Palmer was born at Iwerne Minster in October 1838. At some point after that the family crossed the Atlantic. By 1858 Martha was in Macoupin County, Illinois, where she married Joseph Cullen Drake. Her father died in Macoupin County before 1870. Martha and Joseph eventually moved on to Texas. She died at Goldthwaite, in Mills County, in 1927, aged 88.

Open question: The tree has Martha's mother, Elizabeth, dying in Bath, England, in 1875. Did she go back to England, or is that a different Elizabeth Palmer? A passenger list for the family's crossing would answer it.

What's proven: None of these Dorset records cite a source yet. The Dorset History Centre holds the Stour Provost and Iwerne Minster parish registers. The oldest Lodder generations have a surname mix-up (Lodder and Metyard) that needs sorting out first.

Sarah Leon: birth place changed from "Ohio County Ky" to "unknown". Ohio County, Kentucky didn't exist in 1718.
An Englishman who died in London in 1837 is listed as father of a son born in North Carolina about 1802. No record connects them; it looks like a name match.
Thomas William Creamer lived and died in Bedfordshire, England. No record shows he was the father of a son born in Georgia in 1770.
Sarah Leon (b. 1718) would have been 55 at Thomas's birth, and her husband was born 32 years after her.
Nancy Massey (b. 1775) would have been 53 when Nancy Jane was born in 1828.
William Lodder's parents are listed as a Metyard and a Meatyard, and her father as a Lodder. The surnames don't fit, so two families are probably mixed up.
Part of the same Lodder/Metyard mix-up.
Henry Feigenwinter: death changed. The 1890 Goodspeed sketch says Henry died in 1852. The earlier date, 22 Dec 1845, had no source.
Marriage of Henry Feigenwinter corrected. The 1890 Goodspeed sketch dates the marriage to 1828.
Removed residence dated 1863 for George Thomas Winters: the 1863 Indiana draft registration belongs to a different George Winters; this one lived in Mississippi before and after the war.
Removed the 'Civil War Draft' record from George Thomas Winters: a different George Winters.

Detached James Westly Stewart Esq. from Sir John Stewart & Lady Jane Douglas as parents. The real 4th Baronet of Blair lived c.1726–1797. Lady Jane Douglas married in 1746 at age 48 and had only twin sons, born in 1748, so neither could be the parent of a son born in 1700.

Detached Richard Jarrett from John William Jarrett & Margaret Jane Sherwood as parents. No source supports the 'John William Jarrett, Lord of Derby' ancestry. Richard came to Virginia himself by 1653, which doesn't fit a father settled there since 1620.

Mary replaces Elizabeth Ann Cheney as a parent. Joseph Rentfro's 1772 will and SAR applications name Joshua's mother as Mary. Elizabeth Cheney was born in 1716 and never married into this family. The Cheney, Cole and Weston lines above her (back to 1277) came from a chain of mix-ups.

Detached Antonino Dominici Caruso from Pietro Caruso & Lauria 'Eulalia' Candela as parents. Caruso is one of Sicily's most common surnames. Nothing connects the Termini Imerese Carusos to this Pietro Caruso of Carini, so the 1500s–1600s Carini line came from a name match.
Aaron Brock: birth changed. The 'Cherokee Nation, Cumberland County, Virginia' birthplace combines places hundreds of miles apart.
Aaron Brock: death changed. The Red Bird of the Red Bird River was killed in late 1796 or early 1797, not in 1820.

A 1773 Virginia court record and Clay County compilations name Sukey Brock's husband as Edward Callahan. Their known children are William, Jennie, Elizabeth, Zelphia, Charlotte and Isaac, with no John.
John "Jack" C Callahan: death changed. He doesn't appear on the surviving Tippecanoe muster rolls or casualty lists.
Marriage of John "Jack" C Callahan corrected. 'St. Clair County, Alabama' didn't exist until 1818.
No record yet names Lavica's parents. She may descend from Edward and Sukey Callahan through one of their sons.
Marriage of George R. Haley Sr. corrected. Rockcastle County wasn't formed until 1810. A 1809 marriage bond would be in Lincoln, Pulaski or Madison County.
Marriage of Samuel Doty corrected. Doty-Doten Family in America (1897), p. 283, gives 19 Sep 1700.
William Compton: death changed. The 12 Dec 1815 Woodbridge estate belongs to a different William Compton; the SAR application gives 2 Aug 1815, Somerset County.
Marriage of Joseph Cullen Drake corrected. The Macoupin County record (FHL film 1,320,491) gives 23 Sep 1858.
Detached Elizabeth Worth from Rachel Doty as parents. Rachel Doty would have been 11. Elizabeth Worth's parents are unknown; a Worth family lived in Bernards Township.
Removed 72 people who are no longer connected to the family after the detachments above.
